tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 1
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Three cards are drawn at random without replacement from a standard 52-card deck. The probability of obtaining exactly two aces is greater than $\dfrac{1}{50}$.
Events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A)=0.40$, $P(B)=0.35$, and $P(A \cup B)=0.60$. Then $P(A \cap B)=0.15$.
Events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A)=0.50$, $P(B)=0.40$, and $P(A \cap B)=0.25$. Then $A$ and $B$ are independent.
A discrete random variable $X$ takes values $0$, $1$, and $2$ with probabilities $\dfrac{1}{4}$, $\dfrac{1}{2}$, and $\dfrac{1}{4}$ respectively. Then $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Factory line A makes $60\%$ of items with defect rate $2\%$; line B makes $40\%$ with defect rate $5\%$. Given that a randomly chosen item is defective, the probability it came from line A is greater than $40\%$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

A standard deck has $4$ aces and $48$ non-aces. Drawing $3$ cards without replacement,

$$P(\text{exactly 2 aces}) = \dfrac{\binom{4}{2}\binom{48}{1}}{\binom{52}{3}}$$

$$\binom{4}{2}=6,\quad \binom{48}{1}=48,\quad \binom{52}{3}=22100$$

$$P = \dfrac{288}{22100} = \dfrac{72}{5525} \approx 0.01303$$

while $\dfrac{1}{50}=0.02$. Since $0.01303 < 0.02$, the probability is not greater than $\dfrac{1}{50}$.

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Inclusion-exclusion gives

$$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$$

$$0.60 = 0.40 + 0.35 - P(A \cap B)$$

$$P(A \cap B) = 0.15$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Independence requires $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$.

$$P(A)P(B) = 0.50 \cdot 0.40 = 0.20 \ne 0.25$$

Equivalently, $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{0.25}{0.40} = 0.625 \ne 0.50$.

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$E(X) = 0 \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} + 1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} + 2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} = 1$$

$$E(X^{2}) = 0 + 1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} + 4 \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{2}$$

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = \dfrac{3}{2} - 1^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$

(The SD would be $\sqrt{1/2}$, which is different from the variance.)

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$P(D) = 0.60 \cdot 0.02 + 0.40 \cdot 0.05 = 0.032$$

$$P(A \mid D) = \dfrac{0.012}{0.032} = \dfrac{3}{8} = 0.375$$

That is $37.5\%$, which is not greater than $40\%$.

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: a three-card ace draw without replacement, inclusion-exclusion, an independence test, variance of a three-point law, and two-cause Bayes for a defective item.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 2
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: An urn holds $5$ red and $7$ blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. The probability both are red equals $\dfrac{25}{144}$.
Events $A$, $B$, and $C$ satisfy $P(A)=0.30$, $P(B)=0.40$, $P(C)=0.20$, every pairwise intersection has probability $0.10$, and $P(A \cap B \cap C)=0.05$. Then $P(A \cup B \cup C)=0.65$.
Given $P(A \mid B)=0.60$, $P(B)=0.50$, and $P(A)=0.40$, it follows that $P(B \mid A)=0.75$.
A fair four-sided die yields $X \in \{1,2,3,4\}$ each with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$. Then the standard deviation of $X$ equals $\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{4}}$.

A disease has prior probability $1\%$. A test detects it with sensitivity $99\%$ and has a $2\%$ false-positive rate among healthy people. Given a positive test, the probability the person has the disease is greater than $90\%$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Without replacement,

$$P(\text{both red}) = \dfrac{\binom{5}{2}}{\binom{12}{2}} = \dfrac{10}{66} = \dfrac{5}{33}$$

The claimed $\dfrac{25}{144}=(5/12)^{2}$ is the with-replacement value.

$$\dfrac{5}{33} \approx 0.15152 \ne \dfrac{25}{144} \approx 0.17361$$

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

$$P(A \cup B \cup C) = 0.30+0.40+0.20 - 0.10-0.10-0.10 + 0.05 = 0.65$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$P(A \cap B) = 0.60 \cdot 0.50 = 0.30$$

$$P(B \mid A) = \dfrac{0.30}{0.40} = 0.75$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$E(X)=\dfrac{10}{4}=\dfrac{5}{2},\quad E(X^{2})=\dfrac{30}{4}=\dfrac{15}{2}$$

$$\mathrm{Var}(X)=\dfrac{15}{2}-\dfrac{25}{4}=\dfrac{5}{4}$$

$$\mathrm{SD}(X)=\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{4}}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$P(+) = 0.99\cdot 0.01 + 0.02\cdot 0.99 = 0.0297$$

$$P(D \mid +) = \dfrac{0.0099}{0.0297} = \dfrac{1}{3} \approx 0.333$$

About $33.3\%$, far below $90\%$.

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: an urn draw without replacement versus a with-replacement trap, three-event inclusion-exclusion, reversing a conditional, SD of a fair d4, and Bayes on a rare-disease test.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 3
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: A committee of $4$ is chosen at random from $6$ men and $5$ women. The probability the committee contains exactly $2$ women is $\dfrac{5}{11}$.
One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck and it is a king; it is not replaced. The probability that the next card drawn is also a king equals $\dfrac{1}{13}$.
A game pays $+10$ euros with probability $0.30$ and $-4$ euros with probability $0.70$. The expected payoff of one play is $0.20$ euros.

Three machines produce $50\%$, $30\%$, and $20\%$ of output with defect rates $1\%$, $3\%$, and $4\%$ respectively. Given a defective item, the probability it came from the third machine equals $\dfrac{4}{11}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\binom{11}{4}=330,\quad \binom{5}{2}\binom{6}{2}=150$$

$$P=\dfrac{150}{330}=\dfrac{5}{11}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$P(A \cup B)=0.30+0.50-0.10=0.70 \ne 0.80$$

The claim ignores the intersection (as if the events were disjoint).

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

After one king is removed, $3$ kings remain among $51$ cards:

$$P=\dfrac{3}{51}=\dfrac{1}{17} \ne \dfrac{1}{13}$$

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$E=10\cdot 0.30+(-4)\cdot 0.70=0.2$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$P(D)=0.005+0.009+0.008=0.022$$

$$P(M_{3}\mid D)=\dfrac{0.008}{0.022}=\dfrac{4}{11}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: a mixed-gender committee, a disjoint-union trap, sequential kings without replacement, an expected payoff, and three-cause Bayes.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 4
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Five distinct people are seated uniformly at random in a row of five chairs. The probability that two particular people sit next to each other equals $\dfrac{2}{5}$.
Two fair coins are flipped independently. The probability both land heads equals $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
A random variable $X$ takes values $-1$, $0$, and $1$ with probabilities $0.20$, $0.50$, and $0.30$ respectively. Then $\mathrm{Var}(X)=0.49$.
Emails are spam with probability $20\%$. A filter flags $95\%$ of spam and $5\%$ of ham. Given that a message is flagged, the probability it is spam exceeds $80\%$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Glue the two people into a block ($2$ internal orders) and permute $4$ entities:

$$P=\dfrac{2\cdot 4!}{5!}=\dfrac{48}{120}=\dfrac{2}{5}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$P(A \cap B)=0.70+0.50-0.90=0.30$$

which is not $\le 0.20$.

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$P(\text{HH})=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{4} \ne \dfrac{1}{2}$$

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$E(X)=0.10,\quad E(X^{2})=0.50,\quad \mathrm{Var}(X)=0.49$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$P(+)=0.19+0.04=0.23$$

$$P(\text{spam}\mid +)=\dfrac{0.19}{0.23}=\dfrac{19}{23}\approx 0.826>0.80$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: adjacent seating, recovering an intersection, two-coin independence, variance of a signed law, and spam-filter Bayes.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 5
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Five cards are dealt from a standard 52-card deck. The probability that all five are of the same suit is less than $0.002$.
In a survey, $40\%$ of respondents like tea, $50\%$ like coffee, and $70\%$ like at least one of the two. Then exactly $20\%$ like both tea and coffee.
Suppose $P(A)=0.30$ and $P(A \mid B)=0.20$. Then the occurrence of $B$ makes $A$ more likely than it was unconditionally.
If a discrete random variable $X$ has $\mathrm{Var}(X)=9$, then its standard deviation equals $9$.

Suppliers provide $50\%$, $30\%$, and $20\%$ of parts with good-item rates $98\%$, $95\%$, and $90\%$. Given a good part, the probability it came from the second supplier is approximately $30\%$ (within one percentage point).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$P=\dfrac{4\binom{13}{5}}{\binom{52}{5}}=\dfrac{5148}{2598960}\approx 0.001981 < 0.002$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$0.70=0.40+0.50-P(T\cap C)\Rightarrow P(T\cap C)=0.20$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**C.** → False

$$P(A\mid B)=0.20<0.30=P(A)$$

so $B$ makes $A$ less likely, not more.

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$\mathrm{SD}(X)=\sqrt{9}=3 \ne 9$$

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

$$P(G)=0.955$$

$$P(S_{2}\mid G)=\dfrac{0.285}{0.955}\approx 0.2984$$

about $29.84\%$, within one point of $30\%$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: a five-card same-suit probability, tea/coffee inclusion-exclusion, a decreasing conditional, Var versus SD, and three-supplier Bayes.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 6
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: From a deck of $52$ cards, $2$ cards are drawn without replacement. The probability both are hearts equals $\dfrac{13 \times 12}{52 \times 51}$.
If $P(A)=0.45$, $P(B)=0.55$, and $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, then $P(A \cup B)=0.90$.
A fair die is rolled once. Let $A$ be "even" and $B$ be "at least $4$". Then $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{2}{3}$.
Let $X$ be the number of heads in two independent fair coin tosses. Then $E(X)=1$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
Box 1 has $2$ gold and $1$ silver coins; Box 2 has $1$ gold and $2$ silver. A box is chosen at random, then a coin at random is gold. The probability the box was Box 1 equals $\dfrac{2}{3}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$P=\dfrac{13}{52}\cdot\dfrac{12}{51}=\dfrac{13\times 12}{52\times 51}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Mutually exclusive events satisfy $P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)=0.45+0.55=1$, not $0.90$.

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

$B=\{4,5,6\}$; even members $\{4,6\}$.

$$P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{2}{3}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$E(X)=1,\quad E(X^{2})=\dfrac{3}{2},\quad \mathrm{Var}(X)=\dfrac{1}{2}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$P(G)=\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{3}+\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{3}=\tfrac{1}{2}$$

$$P(B_{1}\mid G)=\dfrac{2}{3}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: two hearts without replacement, mutually exclusive events, a die conditional, two-coin mean/variance, and Bayes on coin boxes.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 7
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: A club has $8$ juniors and $6$ seniors. A team of $3$ is chosen at random. The probability the team has no seniors equals $\dfrac{\binom{8}{3}}{\binom{14}{3}}$.
If $P(A \cup B)=0.80$ and $P(A \cap B)=0.20$, then $P(A)+P(B)=0.60$.
Events with $P(A)=0.40$ and $P(B)=0.50$ must satisfy $P(A \cap B) \ge 0.10$.
For a random variable with $E(X)=4$ and $E(X^{2})=20$, the standard deviation equals $2$.
Prior probabilities of causes $C_{1},C_{2},C_{3}$ are $0.5$, $0.3$, $0.2$ with $P(E \mid C_{i})$ equal to $0.1$, $0.4$, $0.5$. Given $E$, the most probable cause is $C_{1}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

No seniors means all $3$ from $8$ juniors:

$$P=\dfrac{\binom{8}{3}}{\binom{14}{3}}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$P(A)+P(B)=P(A\cup B)+P(A\cap B)=1.00 \ne 0.60$$

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$P(A\cap B)\ge \max(0,P(A)+P(B)-1)=0$$

so the intersection need not be at least $0.10$.

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$\mathrm{Var}(X)=20-16=4,\quad \mathrm{SD}(X)=2$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Unnormalized posteriors: $0.05$, $0.12$, $0.10$. The MAP is $C_{2}$, not $C_{1}$.

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: an all-junior team, rearranging inclusion-exclusion, a Fréchet lower-bound trap, recovering SD, and three-cause MAP Bayes.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 8
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: An urn has $10$ white and $10$ black balls. Three are drawn without replacement. The probability all three are white equals $\dfrac{\binom{10}{3}}{\binom{20}{3}}$.
Two events with $P(A \mid B)=P(A)$ are independent (assuming $P(B)>0$).
A lottery ticket costs $2$ euros and pays $50$ euros with probability $0.01$ (otherwise nothing). The expected net gain is $-1.00$ euros.
Sensors fail with priors $0.1$, $0.2$, $0.7$ and alarm rates $0.9$, $0.6$, $0.1$. Given an alarm under this one-fault model, $P(\text{sensor 3 failed})=0.25<0.4$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$P=\dfrac{\binom{10}{3}}{\binom{20}{3}}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$P(A\cup B)=0.25+0.40-0.10=0.55$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$P(A\mid B)=P(A)$ rearranges to $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**D.** → False

$$E(\text{net})=-2+50\cdot 0.01=-1.5$$

The claim $-1.00$ understates the expected loss.

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

$$P(\text{alarm})=0.28$$

$$P(S_{3}\mid\text{alarm})=\dfrac{0.07}{0.28}=0.25<0.4$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: three white balls, two-event union, conditional independence characterization, lottery expectation, and three-sensor Bayes.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 9
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: From $52$ cards, the number of $5$-card hands that contain exactly $2$ aces is $\binom{4}{2}\binom{48}{3}$.
For any events $A$ and $B$, $P(A \cup B) \le P(A)+P(B)$.
If $\mathrm{Var}(X)=16$, then $\mathrm{Var}(2X)=32$.
A test for a condition with prevalence $5\%$ has sensitivity $100\%$ and specificity $90\%$. Given a positive result, $P(\text{condition} \mid +)$ equals $\dfrac{1}{2.8}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Choose $2$ of $4$ aces and $3$ of $48$ non-aces.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Subadditivity always holds, with equality iff $P(A\cap B)=0$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$P(A\cap B)=0.20$$

$$P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{0.20}{0.50}=0.40$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**D.** → False

$$\mathrm{Var}(2X)=4\cdot 16=64 \ne 32$$

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

$$P(+)=0.05+0.10\cdot 0.95=0.145$$

$$P(C\mid +)=\dfrac{0.05}{0.145}=\dfrac{10}{29}\ne\dfrac{1}{2.8}$$

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: counting two-ace hands, union subadditivity, reversing a conditional, quadratic variance scaling, and a screening posterior trap.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 10
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Four books are arranged at random on a shelf. The probability they appear in a specific predetermined order equals $\dfrac{1}{24}$.
If $P(A)=0.60$ and $P(A \cap B)=0.20$, then $P(B \mid A)=\dfrac{1}{3}$.
Rolling two fair dice, the probability the sum is $7$ equals the probability the sum is $6$.
For $X$ with distribution $P(X=0)=0.2$, $P(X=5)=0.8$, one has $E(X)=4$ and $\mathrm{SD}(X)=2$.
Machines A and B make $70\%$ and $30\%$ of bolts; defect rates $2\%$ and $8\%$. Given a defective bolt, $P(\text{from A}) < P(\text{from B})$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$P=\dfrac{1}{4!}=\dfrac{1}{24}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$P(B\mid A)=\dfrac{0.20}{0.60}=\dfrac{1}{3}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**C.** → False

$$P(\text{sum }=7)=\dfrac{6}{36}\ne\dfrac{5}{36}=P(\text{sum }=6)$$

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

$$E=4,\quad E(X^{2})=20,\quad \mathrm{Var}=4,\quad \mathrm{SD}=2$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$P(A\mid D)=\dfrac{0.014}{0.038}=\dfrac{7}{19}<\dfrac{12}{19}=P(B\mid D)$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: bookshelf order, a definitional conditional, unequal dice sums, a two-point SD, and Bayes comparing machine posteriors.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 11
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: A password uses $3$ distinct digits chosen from $0$–$9$ and arranged in order. The number of such passwords is $\binom{10}{3}=120$.
If $P(A \cap B)=0$ and $P(A)=0.3$, $P(B)=0.4$, then $P(A \cup B)=0.7$.
For independent events with $P(A)=0.2$ and $P(B)=0.5$, one has $P(A \cup B)=0.6$.
If $E(X)=5$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=9$, then $E(X^{2})=34$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Order matters, so the count is the permutation $P(10,3)=10\times 9\times 8=720$, not the combination $\binom{10}{3}=120$.

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Disjoint: $P(A\cup B)=0.7$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$P(A\cup B)=0.2+0.5-0.1=0.6$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$E(X^{2})=9+25=34$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$P(+)=0.019+0.049=0.068$$

$$P(D\mid +)=\dfrac{0.019}{0.068}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: ordered digit passwords, disjoint unions, independent unions, recovering E(X^2), and an explicit Bayes ratio.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 12
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: From $12$ jurors of whom $5$ are women, a subcommittee of $4$ is chosen. The probability of exactly $3$ women is $\dfrac{\binom{5}{3}\binom{7}{1}}{\binom{12}{4}}$.
If $P(A)=0.9$ and $P(B)=0.9$, then it is possible that $P(A \cap B)=0.85$.
A card is drawn from a $52$-card deck. Let $A$ be "ace" and $B$ be "heart". Then $A$ and $B$ are independent.
A random variable with outcomes $10$ and $20$ each with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$ has variance $25$.
Two factories share production $40\%$-$60\%$ with defect rates $3\%$ and $1\%$. Given a good item, the probability it is from the second factory exceeds $0.60$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Hypergeometric probability of exactly $3$ women in $4$ draws.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Feasible range is $[0.8,0.9]$; $0.85$ lies inside.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$P(A)P(B)=\dfrac{1}{13}\cdot\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{1}{52}=P(A\cap B)$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$E=15,\quad E(X^{2})=250,\quad \mathrm{Var}=25$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$P(F_{2}\mid G)=\dfrac{0.594}{0.982}\approx 0.6049 > 0.60$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: a hypergeometric subcommittee, a Fréchet-feasible intersection, ace/heart independence, two-point variance, and Bayes for a good item.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 13
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Choosing a president and a treasurer from $10$ people (roles distinct, one person cannot hold both) can be done in $10 \times 9$ ways.
Given $P(A)=0.30$, $P(B)=0.40$, $P(A \cap B)=0.12$, the events $A$ and $B$ are independent.
For $X$ with $P(X=k)=\dfrac{1}{5}$ for $k=1,\dots,5$, one has $E(X)=3$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\dfrac{5}{2}$.
Spam prior $10\%$; $P(\text{flag}\mid\text{spam})=0.90$, $P(\text{flag}\mid\text{ham})=0.20$. Then $P(\text{spam}\mid\text{flag})=\dfrac{1}{3}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$10\times 9=90$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$P(A\cap B)=0.50+0.45-0.75=0.20$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$P(A)P(B)=0.12=P(A\cap B)$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**D.** → False

$$E(X)=3$$

$$E(X^{2})=11$$

$$\mathrm{Var}(X)=11-9=2 \ne \dfrac{5}{2}$$

The solved result does not agree with the claim, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

$$P(F)=0.27$$

$$P(S\mid F)=\dfrac{0.09}{0.27}=\dfrac{1}{3}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed exam claims: ordered officers, recovering an intersection, product-rule independence, discrete uniform moments, and spam Bayes.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 14
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: An urn contains $4$ red and $6$ green balls. Drawing $2$ with replacement, $P(\text{both red})=\left(\dfrac{4}{10}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{4}{25}$.
If $P(A)=0.35$ and $P(B)=0.25$ are mutually exclusive, then $P(A \cup B)=0.60$.
A fair coin is flipped until the first head. The probability the first head occurs on toss $3$ equals $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3}=\dfrac{1}{8}$.
If $\mathrm{SD}(X)=5$, then $\mathrm{Var}(X)=25$.
Causes $H_{1},H_{2}$ have priors $0.6,0.4$ and $P(D\mid H_{i})=0.3,0.8$. Then $P(H_{2}\mid D)=\dfrac{16}{25}$.

**A.** → True

With replacement: $(4/10)^{2}=4/25$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$P(A\cup B)=0.35+0.25=0.60$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Two tails then a head: $(1/2)^{3}=1/8$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$\mathrm{Var}(X)=5^{2}=25$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$P(D)=0.50$$

$$P(H_{2}\mid D)=\dfrac{0.32}{0.50}=\dfrac{16}{25}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 15
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Without replacement from $5$ red and $5$ blue, $P(\text{first red, second blue})=\dfrac{5}{10}\cdot\dfrac{5}{9}=\dfrac{1}{4}$.

If $P(A\mid B)=0.5$ and $P(B\mid A)=0.5$ with $P(A)=0.4$, then $P(B)=0.4$.
A game: gain $3$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{3}$, lose $1$ with probability $\dfrac{2}{3}$. Then $E(X)=\dfrac{1}{3}$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\dfrac{32}{9}$.

Equal disjoint shares of $0.90$ give $0.30$ each.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$0.5\,P(B)=0.5\cdot 0.4\Rightarrow P(B)=0.4$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

$$E=\dfrac{1}{3},\quad E(X^{2})=\dfrac{11}{3},\quad \mathrm{Var}=\dfrac{32}{9}$$

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

$$P(FN)=0.010+0.006+0.005=0.021$$

Odd faces $1,3,5$; primes among them $3,5$ (since $1$ is not prime).

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 17

Monotonicity plus $A\cap B=A$ when $A\subset B$.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks — 19

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.
